q: In a preemptive scheduler (an RTOS), who stops a running job?
choices: The kernel, on a timer interrupt
The job itself, by returning
The NVIC, when the job's priority drops
The idle task, when it becomes ready
why: Preemptive: the kernel takes the CPU away on the tick. Cooperative (the superloop): the job stops only by returning.

q: A prime-finding loop that never returns is added. What happens under each scheduler?
choices: Superloop: everything freezes. RTOS: the hog is preempted
Superloop: the hog is preempted. RTOS: everything else freezes
Both freeze, because a CPU hog takes every cycle under either scheduler
Both keep working, because SysTick still interrupts the hog in each
why: A cooperative scheduler works only while every job agrees to be short. A preemptive one stops the hog mid-calculation, without its consent, and resumes it later.

q: SysTick still interrupts during a superloop CPU hog. Does that rescue the other superloop jobs?
choices: No: the handler returns to the hog, and no job is switched
Yes: SysTick runs each of the other superloop jobs in turn
Yes: the NVIC preempts the hog once for each waiting job
No: SysTick is masked for as long as the CPU hog keeps running
why: An interrupt alone only counts time; switching to another job needs a kernel that saves one context and restores another. That is what lesson 07 adds.

q: In the measured run, the hog shows 100 % CPU while bar and button show 0 %. Why do bar and button still work?
choices: They preempt the hog within a tick, work briefly, and sleep
They run on a second core while the hog keeps the first one busy
The hog yields to them voluntarily after every prime it finds
They run inside SysTick_Handler, entirely outside the scheduler
why: Higher-priority tasks preempt the hog the moment they are ready. Their work is so short that the per-tick profile charges them 0 %.

q: What is a task's context?
choices: Its registers plus its stack pointer
Its source code together with all of its global variables
Its priority and its current state in the scheduler's lists
Its TCB together with the list of mutexes it currently holds
why: Save the context and the function can be put away; restore it and it continues as if nothing happened.

q: What is a TCB?
choices: The task control block: the kernel's record of one task
The timer control block that drives the tick
The task's copy of the core registers
The table of callbacks for each interrupt
why: os_task_t holds sp, name, prio, base_prio, state, wake and more.

q: Why must sp be the first field of the TCB?
choices: The assembly in PendSV reads it at [tcb + 0]
The C standard requires pointers to come first
The hardware loads PSP from the TCB on exception return
So the TCB is 8-byte aligned for the stack
why: PendSV_Handler is hand-written assembly that loads and stores the saved stack pointer at offset 0 of the TCB. Move the field and the switch breaks silently. The hardware knows nothing about TCBs.

q: Why does the TCB only need to remember the task's saved stack pointer?
choices: Each task's registers are saved on its own stack
The core keeps every task's registers in banked copies
Tasks never use registers other than sp
The registers are saved in a global array indexed by task
why: Each task has its own stack and its registers live there while it is switched out; the TCB just points at them.

q: How many words of context does one switched-out task keep on its stack?
why: 8 words pushed by the hardware (r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR) plus 8 saved by PendSV (r4–r11).

q: Five tasks are created. How many bytes of forged context does os_task_create write in total?
choices: 320 bytes
160 bytes
80 bytes
640 bytes
why: Each forged frame is 16 words = 64 bytes (8 for the hardware frame, 8 for r4–r11); 5 × 64 = 320.

q: Which stack pointer do exception handlers use?
choices: MSP, always
PSP, always
Whichever the interrupted task used
PSP if CONTROL.SPSEL = 1
why: Handlers always run on MSP. CONTROL.SPSEL = 1 only selects PSP for Thread mode.

q: When do tasks run on PSP?
choices: In Thread mode with CONTROL.SPSEL = 1
In Handler mode with CONTROL.SPSEL = 0
Whenever PRIMASK is set
Only after a HardFault
why: PSP is the process stack for Thread mode when SPSEL = 1; main() after reset uses MSP.

q: Why do handlers never need room on a task's stack beyond the 8-word frame?
choices: Handlers run on MSP, a stack no task owns
Handlers are forbidden from using local variables
The NVIC allocates handler stacks in the TCB
Handlers push their registers onto PSP, then switch
why: The hardware frame goes on the interrupted task's stack; everything the handler does after that uses MSP. Each task's stack only has to hold that task.

q: What does EXC_RETURN = 0xFFFFFFFD mean?
choices: Return to Thread mode, use PSP
Return to Thread mode, use MSP
Return to Handler mode
Return in ARM state
why: 0xFFFFFFFD is Thread/PSP, the value every switch in this kernel returns with. 0xFFFFFFF9 is Thread/MSP and 0xFFFFFFF1 is Handler mode.

q: What does EXC_RETURN = 0xFFFFFFF9 mean?
choices: Return to Thread mode, use MSP
Return to Thread mode, use PSP
Return to Handler mode, use MSP
A fault on the process stack
why: 0xFFFFFFF9: Thread mode on MSP, as main() uses after reset.

q: Which bit of EXC_RETURN says 'use PSP', and what is it in 0xFFFFFFF9?
choices: Bit 2; it is 0, so MSP
Bit 2; it is 1, so PSP
Bit 3; it is 1, so PSP
Bit 0; it is 1, so Thumb
why: D = 1101 has bit 2 set (PSP); 9 = 1001 has it clear (MSP). Bit 3 is the Thread/Handler bit.

q: A HardFault handler reads lr = 0xFFFFFFF1. Who faulted?
choices: A handler, on MSP
A task, on PSP
main(), in Thread mode on MSP
The kernel's idle task
why: 0xFFFFFFF1 is Handler mode, and its bit 2 is clear, so the frame is on MSP. A task fault would show 0xFFFFFFFD.

q: How are xPSR, MSP, PSP, PRIMASK and CONTROL reached?
choices: Only with mrs and msr: they have no memory address
With ordinary ldr and str at fixed addresses inside the SCB
With ldr and str at 0xE000E000 and the words just after it
Only from Handler mode, through a request made to the NVIC
why: They live inside the core, outside the memory map. CMSIS wraps the instructions as __get_PSP(), __set_PRIMASK() and so on.

q: A FreeRTOS port for the M3 uses BASEPRI to mask only some interrupts. What does the M0+ offer?
choices: Only PRIMASK: no BASEPRI or FAULTMASK on this core
BASEPRI as well, at exactly the same address as on the Cortex-M3
FAULTMASK, which masks every interrupt except NMI by priority
BASEPRI, but it can only be written while in Handler mode
why: The M0+ has PRIMASK alone; CMSIS compiles BASEPRI and FAULTMASK only for Thumb-2 cores.

q: What does CONTROL read while a task runs in this kernel?
choices: 0x00000000: MSP, privileged
0x00000003: PSP, unprivileged
why: SPSEL (bit 1) = 1 means Thread mode uses PSP. The kernel never writes CONTROL; the exception return with 0xFFFFFFFD sets SPSEL.

q: Where is the SCB, and which two of its registers does the kernel use?
choices: 0xE000ED00; ICSR and SHPR3
0xE000E100; ISER and IPR
0xE000ED00; VTOR and AIRCR
0xE000E010; CTRL and LOAD
why: The System Control Block is part of the core at 0xE000ED00. ICSR pends PendSV; SHPR3 holds the PendSV and SysTick priorities. 0xE000E100 is the NVIC; 0xE000E010 is SysTick.

q: ICSR is at offset 0x04 in the SCB and PENDSVSET is bit 28. What is the write that pends PendSV?
why: 1 << 28 = 0x10000000, written to 0xE000ED00 + 4. 0x08000000 is bit 27, PENDSVCLR.

q: Why is PendSV pended with SCB->ICSR = PENDSVSET and not |=?
choices: ICSR is write-1-to-act; zeros do nothing
|= would also set PENDSVCLR, which would cancel the request at once
ICSR is a write-only register, so the read in |= would fault
|= is three instructions, so an interrupt could split it and lose the bit
why: In ICSR writing 1 acts and writing 0 does nothing. A |= reads back status bits and writes them as requests, which is wrong for a write-1-to-act register.

q: SHPR3 holds SysTick at bits 31:30 and PendSV at 23:22. With both at priority 3, what does SHPR3 read?
why: 3 << 30 = 0xC0000000 and 3 << 22 = 0x00C00000; together 0xC0C00000. 0xC0000000 is lesson 06, where only SysTick was set.

q: What are PendSV's two defining properties in this kernel?
choices: Pended by software, and given the lowest priority
Raised by SysTick, and given the highest priority
Pended by software, and given the highest priority
Raised by any IRQ, and given SysTick's priority
why: Only software sets its pending bit, and at priority 3 it runs only when no other handler is active.

q: Why must a context switch never happen inside another interrupt handler?
choices: The handler's half-finished frame would return into the wrong task
Handlers run unprivileged and so are not allowed to write PSP at all
The NVIC forbids the msr instruction anywhere inside a handler
SysTick would lose a tick for every switch made inside a handler
why: Swapping the task beneath a running handler would return that handler into the wrong world. So the switch is deferred to PendSV, which runs only when nothing else is active.

q: Where does the actual context switch happen?
choices: Only in PendSV_Handler
In SysTick_Handler, after the tick
In schedule(), wherever it is called
In the ISR that made a task ready
why: Deciding (schedule()) happens anywhere: the tick, os_delay, mutex unlock, queue put. Switching happens in one place only, PendSV.

q: schedule() has pended PendSV, then decides the current task should keep running after all. What can it do?
choices: Write PENDSVCLR to cancel the switch
Nothing: a pended PendSV always runs
Raise PendSV's priority to 0 to finish it early
Return 0xFFFFFFF9 instead of 0xFFFFFFFD
why: Deciding can change its mind with PENDSVCLR; once PendSV runs, the switch happens.

q: Besides SysTick, which calls run schedule() and can lead to a switch?
choices: os_delay, mutex unlock and queue put, in tasks and ISRs
Only os_task_create, and only before the scheduler has started
None of them: only the tick is allowed to decide on a switch
Only HardFault_Handler, when it needs to recover a crashed task
why: A task that sleeps or blocks does not wait for the tick to be switched out; it joins the flow at the decision step.

q: When task A is interrupted, which registers does the hardware push onto A's stack?
choices: r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR
r0–r12 and lr
Only pc and xPSR
why: The hardware pushes 8 words, half the context. PendSV saves the other half, r4–r11.

q: What does PendSV_Handler save for the old task?
choices: r4–r11 on the old task's stack, and its SP in the TCB
r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR, all pushed onto the MSP stack
All sixteen registers, copied word by word into the TCB itself
r4–r11 on MSP, and the old task's SP kept in the CONTROL register
why: The hardware already pushed r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR; PendSV pushes the callee-saved r4–r11 beside them and stores the SP into the TCB.

q: How does task B's pc get restored at the end of a switch?
choices: The hardware pops B's 8-word frame on exception return
PendSV loads it explicitly with an ldr pc, [r0] instruction
SysTick_Handler branches to it after deciding B should run
pick() calls B's task function directly, as an ordinary function
why: PendSV restores B's r4–r11, sets PSP to B's hardware frame and returns with 0xFFFFFFFD; the hardware pops r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR.

q: Put the switch from A to B in order.
choices: Hardware pushes A's half → SysTick decides → PendSV pended → PendSV saves A, loads B → hardware pops B
PendSV pended → hardware pushes A's half → SysTick decides → hardware pops B → PendSV saves A
SysTick decides → PendSV saves A → hardware pushes A's half → PendSV pended → hardware pops B
Hardware pushes A's half → PendSV saves A, loads B → SysTick decides → PendSV pended → hardware pops B
why: Hardware entry, decide, pend, PendSV runs when nothing else is active, the switch itself, then the exception return pops B.

q: PendSV runs: PSP = 0x20001040 (A's hardware frame). It stores tcb->sp = PSP − 32. What is stored?
why: 0x1040 − 0x20 = 0x1020. 32 bytes is room for the 8 words r4–r11 below the hardware frame.

q: How big is this kernel's PendSV_Handler?
choices: 34 instructions, 88 bytes
8 instructions, 16 bytes
about 300 instructions
16 instructions, 64 bytes
why: 34 instructions and 88 bytes including its literal pool: the whole of multitasking.

q: Why does the M0+ kernel copy r8–r11 into r4–r7 before storing them?
choices: Thumb-1 stm/ldm reach only r0–r7
r8–r11 cannot be read in Handler mode
r8–r11 belong to the hardware frame
Storing high registers would misalign PSP
why: stmia has an 8-bit register list, r0–r7 only. stmia {r4-r11} exists on the M3, not here. mov between low and high registers is allowed.

q: On restore, why are r8–r11 restored first and r4–r7 last?
choices: r4–r7 carry r8–r11 through the copy, so they load last
r8–r11 are the callee-saved registers, so AAPCS wants them back first
The hardware pops r4–r7 automatically afterwards on exception return
The ldm instruction can only load the high registers before the low ones
why: r8–r11 are restored by loading them into r4–r7 and moving them up. Loading the real r4–r7 last keeps that copy from being overwritten.

q: A new task has never run. How does the first switch to it work?
choices: os_task_create forges the stack it would have if interrupted
PendSV calls the task function directly, just the first time round
The hardware builds a frame automatically when PSP is first loaded
The idle task starts it with a branch-with-link to its first line
why: A forged frame makes a brand-new task look exactly like one preempted a second ago, so the switch code needs no special case.

q: What xPSR value is forged into every new task's frame?
choices: 0xFFFFFFFD
why: Only the Thumb bit, bit 24. 0x61000000 is a stacked xPSR with flags too; 0xFFFFFFFD is EXC_RETURN.

q: os_task_create forges xPSR = 0x00000000 by mistake. What happens?
choices: The task HardFaults on its first switch
It runs normally; xPSR flags start at zero anyway
It runs in ARM state, more slowly
It runs, but its interrupts are masked
why: A clear T bit asks for ARM state, which the M0+ does not have, so the return faults at once.

q: In the forged frame, where does the task's argument go, and why?
choices: The r0 slot, because AAPCS passes the first argument in r0
The r4 slot, because r4 is callee-saved and survives the switch
The lr slot, so that the task can return to its argument later
The TCB, because the forged stack is reserved for registers only
why: When the hardware pops the frame, r0 holds arg and the task receives it as a normal parameter.

q: Why is the forged lr set to task_exit?
choices: So a task that returns is parked, not lost in memory
So the first switch to the task can find its TCB
Because EXC_RETURN must already be in lr when the first switch happens
So the task restarts from its first line each time it finishes
why: If the task function ever returns, it lands in task_exit and is parked for good.

q: In the forged frame, what goes in the pc slot?
choices: The task function's address
task_exit
0xFFFFFFFD
The TCB's address
why: pc = the task function, lr = task_exit, r0 = the argument, xPSR = 0x01000000, zeros elsewhere.

q: Which task does pick() run?
choices: The highest-priority READY task, round-robin among equals
The task that has waited longest, whatever its priority happens to be
The lowest-priority READY task, so that it eventually gets a turn
The task with the most unused stack still left, to spread the load
why: Fixed-priority preemptive plus round-robin among equal priorities, one tick each.

q: READY tasks: bar (prio 2), hog (prio 1), report (prio 1), idle (prio 0). button (prio 3) is SLEEPING. Who runs?
choices: bar
button
hog or report, in turn
idle
why: button is not READY, so it is not a candidate. bar has the highest priority of the READY tasks.

q: Only hog (prio 1), report (prio 1) and idle (prio 0) are READY, and hog is running. What happens over the next ticks?
choices: hog and report alternate, one tick each
hog keeps running until it blocks
report runs to completion, then hog
idle runs, because the others are equal
why: pick() starts its search after the current task and only a strictly higher priority replaces a find, so equals take turns.

q: A (prio 2) and B (prio 2) are READY, C (prio 3) is BLOCKED on a mutex, and A is running. Who runs after the next tick?
choices: B
A again
C
idle
why: C is not READY, so it cannot be picked. Among the equal-priority READY tasks the search starts after A, so B gets the next tick.

q: Why does pick() always find a task to run?
choices: Idle, priority 0, is always READY
SysTick makes every task READY at each tick
pick() returns the current task if nothing is found
A sleeping task counts as ready for pick()
why: The idle task never sleeps or blocks, so there is always an answer.

q: On this chip, which numbering treats a larger number as more urgent?
choices: The kernel's task priorities (like FreeRTOS)
The NVIC's interrupt priorities
Both
Neither: 0 is most urgent everywhere
why: Kernel: higher number, more urgent. NVIC: 0 is most urgent. Two numberings on one chip; always say which you mean.

q: A task has priority 3 and an IRQ has NVIC priority 3. Which statement is right?
choices: The task is the most urgent task; the IRQ the least urgent IRQ
Both are the most urgent of their kind, so the IRQ and task tie
Both are the least urgent of their kind, so both always wait
They are equal in rank, so the IRQ cannot preempt the task at all
why: 3 is the top task priority here (button) but the lowest NVIC priority. Any enabled interrupt preempts any task anyway: tasks run in Thread mode.

q: A task calls os_delay(10). Which state is it in, and what makes it leave?
choices: SLEEPING, until the tick reaches its wake time
BLOCKED, until another task unlocks
READY, but skipped for 10 ticks
SLEEPING, until a queue item arrives
why: SLEEPING waits for a time; BLOCKED waits for a thing (a mutex, a queue).

q: A task calls os_queue_get() on an empty queue. What state is it in?
choices: BLOCKED
SLEEPING
READY
Running, spinning on the queue
why: Waiting for a thing is BLOCKED; it leaves when an item arrives.

q: The tick is at 0xFFFFFFF0 and a task's wake is 0x00000005. The kernel tests (int32_t)(ticks − wake) >= 0. Does it wake?
choices: No: the difference is −21, so 21 ticks to go
Yes: 0xFFFFFFF0 is far larger than 5
Yes: the difference is 4 294 967 275
No: it never wakes across the wrap
why: ticks − wake = 0xFFFFFFEB, which as int32_t is −21. The signed difference is wrap-safe, so the task wakes 21 ticks later, after the counter wraps.

q: Which state is the currently running task in?
choices: READY: it is the READY task pick() chose
RUNNING, a fourth state that only one task can be in at a time
BLOCKED, because it is the one holding the CPU at the moment
SLEEPING until the next tick, when pick() chooses again
why: The kernel has three states. Running is not separate; it is the READY task that os_current points at.

q: A task waits for 50 ms by spinning on millis(). What does that cost compared with os_delay(50)?
choices: Spinning: 100 % CPU, nobody lower runs. Sleeping: off the CPU
The same cost: both of them use the SysTick tick to wait 50 ms
Less: spinning avoids the two context switches that sleeping needs
More stack for the spinning task, but exactly the same CPU time
why: A busy-waiting task holds the CPU; a sleeping one is off the CPU and every other READY task runs.

q: What does os_delay_until(&last, period) give that os_delay(period) does not?
choices: A fixed grid: wake times don't drift with the task's work
Shorter latency, because the wake-up skips the tick entirely
Permission to call it from an ISR as well as from a task
A busy-wait for periods that are shorter than a single tick
why: Like lesson 06's += period: the task wakes on a fixed grid however long its work took. The LED bar stays exactly 60 ms apart.

q: The bar task uses os_delay_until(&last, 60). last = 1000 and its work took 7 ms. When does it next wake?
choices: At tick 1060
At tick 1067
At tick 1053
At tick 1120
why: os_delay_until keeps the grid: last + period = 1060, however long the work took. os_delay(60) after the work would give 1067.

q: The per-task tick count charges one millisecond to whoever was running at each tick. What is that technique?
choices: Statistical profiling of CPU share
Exact cycle counting
Deadline monitoring
Stack high-water measurement
why: Sampled at each tick, over a second it gives each task's CPU share, the cpu% column of the report.

q: Over one second (1000 ticks) the hog was running at 700 ticks and idle at 300. What CPU shares does the report show?
choices: hog 70 %, idle 30 %
hog 100 %, idle 0 %
hog 30 %, idle 70 %
hog 7 %, idle 3 %
why: Each tick charges 1 ms to the task running then: 700 / 1000 = 70 %.

q: In one second the report task was running at 50 of the 1000 ticks. What cpu% does the report print for it?
why: Statistical profiling charges one tick (1 ms) to whoever was running: 50 / 1000 = 5 %.

q: The button task wakes 200 times a second and the bar about 17. Each visit is a switch in and a switch out. About how many switches a second?
choices: About 430
About 217
About 870
About 1000
why: (200 + 17) × 2 ≈ 434; the measured figure was about 420.

q: Who is held up by masking interrupts with PRIMASK, and who by a mutex?
choices: PRIMASK: everything. Mutex: only tasks wanting that resource
PRIMASK: only lower-priority tasks. Mutex: every task and every interrupt
Both hold up only the tasks that actually use the shared data
PRIMASK: only interrupts, never tasks. Mutex: only the idle task
why: Masking freezes the whole system, so it is for a few instructions. A mutex can last as long as the work takes, and a waiter is BLOCKED, off the CPU.

q: Why can't an interrupt handler call os_mutex_lock()?
choices: Locking may block, and a handler has nothing to put to sleep
Handlers run on MSP, and a stack pointer on MSP cannot own a mutex
Handlers run unprivileged, so they cannot change PRIMASK inside lock
It would deadlock SysTick, which is the owner of every mutex
why: Locking may have to wait, which means putting the caller to sleep. An ISR has nothing to put to sleep, so it must use non-blocking APIs such as os_queue_put_from_isr().

q: What protects the mutex's own bookkeeping inside os_mutex_lock()?
choices: Masking interrupts for a few instructions
A second, smaller mutex nested inside the first one
PendSV's lowest priority, which keeps every handler out
Nothing at all: the owner field is a single atomic word
why: enter() and leave() save and restore PRIMASK around the owner check. The mutex makes a long critical section cheap, built on a short masked one.

q: High needs a mutex Low holds; Medium, which doesn't use it, preempts Low. What is High waiting for?
choices: Medium, a task it outranks
Low only, for its 30 ms
The idle task
The SysTick handler
why: Low cannot run to release the mutex while Medium runs, so High in effect waits for Medium: priority inversion.

q: High waits for Low's mutex during Low's 30 ms critical section, with no Medium running. Is that priority inversion?
choices: No: that is blocking, expected and bounded
Yes: any wait on a lower task is inversion
Yes, and it is unbounded
No: High never waits for a lower task
why: Blocking (High waits for Low) is legitimate. Inversion is waiting behind a task that does not hold the resource; unbounded inversion lasts as long as Medium runs.

q: Which famous system suffered priority inversion, and when?
choices: Mars Pathfinder, 1997
Apollo 11, 1969
Ariane 5, 1996
Therac-25, 1985
why: Pathfinder kept resetting because a high-priority bus task was starved; it was fixed remotely by enabling priority inheritance.

q: How does priority inheritance fix inversion?
choices: Low runs at High's priority while holding the mutex High wants
High's priority is lowered to Low's until the mutex becomes free again
Medium is suspended by the kernel whenever any task holds any mutex
Interrupts are masked with PRIMASK for as long as Low holds the mutex
why: Medium can no longer preempt Low; Low finishes, unlocks and returns to base_prio.

q: On unlock, what priority does the former holder return to?
choices: Its base_prio
The waiter's priority
0, the idle priority
The highest priority in the system
why: The TCB keeps base_prio for exactly this.

q: Low (prio 1) holds the mutex; High (prio 3) blocks on it; Mid is prio 2. With inheritance, at what priority does Low now run?
choices: 3, until it unlocks
1, its base_prio
2, just above Mid's
4, above everyone
why: Low borrows its waiter's priority, 3, so Mid (2) can no longer preempt it. On unlock it returns to base_prio 1.

q: Low holds the mutex for 30 ms; Mid computes for 120 ms. Measured worst waits for High: 10 ms with inheritance and 110 ms without. Why is any wait over 40 ms a sign of inversion here?
choices: It exceeds Low's 30 ms hold, so High was waiting behind Mid
40 ms is the tick period, so any longer wait means a missed tick
Mid's period is 40 ms, so a longer wait shows Mid had already finished
It exceeds High's own 100 ms deadline, so the system reports a failure
why: Legitimate blocking is bounded by Low's 30 ms. Anything well beyond it was time spent behind Mid. With inheritance there were none.

q: What limitation does the lesson admit about its priority inheritance?
choices: It is right for one mutex at a time, not nested holds
It works only for tasks of priority 0 and 1
It works only when interrupts are masked
It raises the holder's priority permanently
why: A task holding two mutexes with different waiters needs a real implementation; FreeRTOS's is several hundred lines.

q: How does a queue differ from a mutex for sharing data?
choices: A queue copies the data out; a mutex guards data that stays shared
A queue is faster than a mutex but only works between two ISRs
A queue can hold only one item, while a mutex can protect many
A queue never blocks its caller, while a mutex always blocks
why: Copy instead of share. put blocks while full, get blocks while empty.

q: What does os_queue_put_from_isr() do when the queue is full?
choices: Returns 0 at once; it never blocks
Blocks the ISR until a slot frees
Overwrites the oldest item
Pends PendSV and retries
why: A handler has no task to put to sleep, so it reports 'full' and lets the handler decide (lesson 08 counts it as dropped).

q: os_queue_put_from_isr() makes a waiting task READY. When does that task actually run?
choices: When the last handler returns, via PendSV
Immediately, from inside the ISR that made it ready
Only at the next SysTick tick, when pick() is run again
When the ISR calls the task's function directly at the end
why: It calls schedule(), which pends PendSV; the switch happens the moment no handler is active.

q: In both FreeRTOS and this kernel, what is the ISR-safe queue put called?
choices: xQueueSendFromISR / os_queue_put_from_isr
xQueueSend / os_queue_put
vTaskDelayUntil / os_delay_until
xTaskCreate / os_task_create
why: xTaskCreate, vTaskDelayUntil and xQueueSendFromISR correspond to os_task_create, os_delay_until and os_queue_put_from_isr.

q: How does the kernel find each task's high-water mark?
choices: It fills each stack with 0xDEADBEEF and counts untouched words
It records the lowest stack pointer it sees at every SysTick tick
The MPU traps the deepest access each task makes to its own stack
The compiler reports each task's maximum stack use in the map file
why: The stack grows down; words still reading 0xDEADBEEF at the bottom were never reached. Exercise every path, read it, add a margin.

q: A 128-word task stack still has 104 words reading 0xDEADBEEF. What is its high-water mark?
choices: 24 words (96 bytes)
104 words
24 bytes
128 words
why: 128 − 104 = 24 words used, as measured for the bar task.

q: Stacks of 128, 128, 128, 512 and 64 words are allocated. What fraction of the 12 KB SRAM is that?

About 8 % (960 bytes)
About 63 % (7680 bytes)
About 16 % (1920 bytes)
why: 960 words × 4 = 3840 bytes, and 3840 / 12 288 ≈ 31 %. 960 bytes forgets that a word is 4 bytes.

q: The report task needs 115 words but is given a 96-word stack. How far does it overflow?

q: What does a stack overflow usually look like on an MCU like this?
choices: Another task's data quietly wrong, far from the cause
An immediate HardFault, reported in the task that overflowed
A reset by the watchdog a few milliseconds after the overflow
A compiler warning about the stack size at build time
why: Measured: the report task overflowed by 19 words into the hog's primes counter, which then read 536 871 010 (a stack address). Nothing crashed.

q: After the overflow, the primes counter read 536 871 010. What is that in hex, and why is it telling?
choices: 0x20000062: an SRAM address, written by a stack
0x08000062: a flash address, from the code
0xDEADBEEF: the fill pattern was overwritten
0x00000062: only the low byte changed
why: 536 871 010 = 0x20000062, inside SRAM at 0x20000000: a stack value in another task's variable.

q: In the stacked exception frame, which word is the faulting pc?
choices: Word 6
Word 0
Word 7
Word 5
why: The frame is r0, r1, r2, r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR: pc is word 6 (counting from 0), at SP + 24.

q: A task faults and its hardware frame starts at PSP = 0x20000F00. At which address is the stacked pc?
why: The frame is r0, r1, r2, r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR; pc is word 6, at +24 = 0x18. 0x20000F1C is xPSR and 0x20000F14 is lr.

q: How does the HardFault handler know which stack holds the frame?
choices: Bit 2 of LR (EXC_RETURN): 1 means PSP
Bit 24 of the stacked xPSR: 1 means the frame is on PSP
CONTROL.nPRIV: 1 means an unprivileged task was the one that faulted
The fault-status register names which stack the frame was pushed to
why: EXC_RETURN in LR says which stack was in use. The M0+ has no fault-status registers.

q: What can the M0+'s HardFault report tell you, and what not?
choices: Where it faulted (pc, via addr2line), but not why
Why it faulted, from CFSR, but not where
Both where and why, from the stacked frame
Neither: the frame is lost on the M0+
why: No fault-status registers on the M0+, so the reason is lost. The Cortex-M4 in lesson 11 has CFSR.

q: A stacked xPSR reads 0x61000000. Which bits are set?
choices: Z, C and the Thumb bit
N, Z and the Thumb bit
Only the Thumb bit
C, V and the Thumb bit
why: 0x6 in bits 31:28 is 0110: Z (30) and C (29); 0x01 in bits 27:24 is T (24).

q: Why is this RTOS's context switch only tens of cycles while a desktop OS takes microseconds?
choices: No MMU address space, FPU state or TLB to switch
The M0+ runs at a higher clock rate than a desktop CPU does
It saves only 2 registers per switch instead of all 16 of them
It skips saving the stack pointer, because each task has its own
why: Leaving out the MMU, FPU and TLB makes it cheap, and is also why one bad pointer in any task can overwrite every other task.
